segments.text: Acid–base chemistry is one of the most frequently applied frameworks in all of chemistry, from biological buffer systems to industrial processes, and builds directly on the equilibrium concepts introduced in Thermodynamics and Kinetics.
Three progressively broader definitions of acids and bases are used depending on context. The
definition (an acid produces H⁺ in water, a base produces OH⁻) works only for aqueous solutions. The
definition (an acid is a proton donor, a base is a proton acceptor) is broader, covering non-aqueous and gas-phase reactions. The

definition (an acid is an electron-pair acceptor, a base is an electron-pair donor) is the broadest, encompassing reactions with no protons involved at all — such as the formation of coordinate bonds in complex ions (Chapter 8, Chapter 10).

A larger Ka means a stronger (more dissociated) weak acid. Ka and Kb for a conjugate pair are related through the water autoionization constant, Kw = Ka × Kb.

items.text: Three acid–base definitions (Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry, Lewis) apply in progressively broader contexts, with Lewis being general enough to describe coordinate bond formation.
Strong acids/bases dissociate completely; weak ones establish an equilibrium described by Ka/Kb, with a strong-acid/weak-conjugate-base inverse relationship.
pH, pOH, and pKa compress concentration ranges logarithmically, with pH = pKa marking the half-neutralisation point of a weak acid.
Buffers (via the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation) resist pH change; titration curves reveal the equivalence point and distinguish strong versus weak acid–base systems by their shape.
